title: Adéla (singer)
notes: Born 2003-11-27, Bratislava (also in AD-S22), so not c. 2004 as the brief said. Dream Academy 2023, eliminated early; signed to Capitol May 2025; EP The Provocateur August 2025; first Slovak artist on the Billboard Hot 100. The page claims she calls her lyrics exaggerated, over-the-top versions of her life, citing The FADER 2025-08-25. Re-checking that FADER page (AD-S38) found no such wording, so the claim is UNSUPPORTED and not used. Chart table lists 'Nicole Kidman' UK peak 50, which conflicts with AD-S50 (No. 4) and is probably stale.

title: Student Becomes Master: ADÉLA Interviewed
locator: opening section; EP section; SexOnTheBeat section; album section
notes: She had an aversion to writing about love and PRIMA brought her to love songs. She wanted songs that are witty, young and girly but also smart and deep, covering love, family, sex and insecurity about sex. Clash paraphrases advice from Slatkin and Brady: writing to what people want makes the worst art. Fluent in English by about age 9 via the Disney Channel and celebrity interviews. Born 2003-11-27, Bratislava. Says nothing about who co-wrote which song.

title: Adéla - Ain't in LA
notes: Average 5.76 from 17 critics (range 3-10). Main disagreements: vague or patronising lyrics versus a great chorus; the 'We Can't Stop' and 'Royals' echoes as asset versus flaw; the Slovak angle moving versus not specific enough.

title: The baddest bitches ain't in LA, they're in Vogue. Cover star of the September Issue, Adéla
locator: Q&A: writing process; creative blocks; collaborators; KGB; Ain't in LA; Slovak directness; Red Bottoms
notes: The best source on her process. Ideas start in solitude; she prefers scheduled co-writes, talking through ideas, melodies and memories; they write many bad songs to reach good ones. Slatkin is a very close collaborator; she has written a lot with Julia Michaels and Billy Walsh; Rachel Sennott named the album. 'Red Bottoms' came from a worn-out shoe. 'KGB' was literal and partly comic, so she added a Ukraine disclaimer. LA is used as a metaphor. Slovaks speak directly while Americans circle the point. One track is her frustration and sadness on a loop. No Theron Thomas, nothing on writing in a second language and no changed lines.

title: ADÉLA wants to make you uncomfortable
notes: Covers the EP era, not PRIMA. Teaching herself English by 9 (para 5). Grimes found 'HOMEWRECKED' and asked who sang the harmonies; she did (para 12). EP producers: Alex Chapman, Zhone, Dylan Brady, Grimes. Provocation as a way of controlling her own story. Re-checked: the page does NOT contain the exaggerated or over-the-top wording that Wikipedia (AD-S5) attributes to it.

title: Adela - Prima (user review)
notes: 3.0/5. Says she has not yet learned to write convincingly sincere lyrics; mid-tempo songs and ballads are not her strength; 'Hitachi' and 'Therapy' are a slog; 'Ain't In LA' has a great singalong hook; the shift from The Provocateur's electropop is puzzling. User review, so weight it low.

title: 'PRIMA' album review: Is ADÉLA this year's 'Best New Artist?'
notes: 3.5/5. 'Red Bottoms' shows her writing best (para 4). The 'I'm The Man' concept is too familiar (para 11). 'Hitachi' is too close to Ariana Grande (para 13). 'Therapy' is hard to endure vocally (para 19). The album wears its influences too openly and is a step back from the EP (para 21).

title: Review: ADÉLA steps into the spotlight with debut album 'PRIMA'
notes: 9/10, uniformly positive. 'KGB' covers learning English and compares her to a spy (para 3). 'Red Bottoms' asks whether she would still be loved with her imperfections (para 6). Lara Raj interlude on 'Boys'.

title: PRIMA review (Pipe Dream)
material_accessed: html text (no byline or date visible)
notes: 4/5. Reads 'Hitachi', 'Fantasize' and 'Starving Artist' as a narrative trilogy (para 9). 'Therapy' reads like a diary and its lyrics are especially simple (para 10). Reports fans finding the shift tamer and more on-the-nose than her provocative earlier work (para 12).

title: ADÉLA - PRIMA (Album Review)
notes: B+. On 'Boys', spoken exchanges with Lara Raj break up the verses and choruses, and male attention is compared to a vending machine. 'Hitachi' is about missing intimacy. 'KGB' casts her as a spy in the US industry and covers learning English and her Dream Academy elimination. Small blog.
